\chapter{The Letter in the Way}
\label{ch:bn-the-letter-in-the-way}
\hlchaptermodality{31}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can say the shirt, a shirt and another shirt — because the letter \bn{ট} finally exists and the classifier that does the work of the exists with it.}

Sixty nouns taught across chapters ten to fifteen — a pantry, a family, a face and a wardrobe — become pickable-out for the first time: the shirt, a shirt, another shirt, and the polite form for people.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[ṭô]{\bn{ট} — the fourth corner}

\label{lesson:BN-W05-tta}



\begin{quote}
Write \textbf{\bn{ত}}, then \textbf{\bn{দ}}, then \textbf{\bn{ড}}. Say for each one where the tongue goes and whether the voice is on.

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Recall:} two chapters back, the joiner that puts one event beside another — \emph{jôkhon}
\end{itemize}
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Script}
\begin{quote}
\bn{ট}
\end{quote}

You have been carrying three corners of a square without being shown the square.

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{} & \textbf{voice off} & \textbf{voice on} \\
\midrule
\textbf{tongue on the teeth} & \textbf{\bn{ত}} \emph{tô} & \textbf{\bn{দ}} \emph{dô} \\
\textbf{tongue curled back} & \textbf{\bn{ট}} \emph{ṭô} & \textbf{\bn{ড}} \emph{ḍô} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

Two switches, four letters. \textbf{\bn{ট}} is the one the book never filled in: the tongue curled back to the ridge, exactly where you put it for \textbf{\bn{ড}}, and the voice switched off, exactly as you do for \textbf{\bn{ত}}. If you can make the other three you can already make this one — you have never been asked to.

An English \emph{t} lands between the two rows, which is the same trap \textbf{\bn{দ}} and \textbf{\bn{ড}} set. To an English ear \textbf{\bn{ত}} and \textbf{\bn{ট}} are one letter. They are not, and they spell different words.

With the mātrā:

\begin{quote}
\textbf{\bn{ট}} + \textbf{\bn{া}} $\to$ \textbf{\bn{টা}}
\end{quote}

Hold on to that syllable. It is the shape of the next four lessons, and it is the reason this letter could not wait any longer.

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Write it:} \bn{ট}
  \item \emph{Write it:} \bn{টা}
  \item \emph{Say it:} \textbf{\bn{ত}} then \textbf{\bn{ট}} — teeth, then curled back, voice off for both
  \item \emph{Say it:} \textbf{\bn{ট}} then \textbf{\bn{ড}} — curled back for both, voice off then on
  \item \emph{Write it:} \bn{ত} \bn{ট} \bn{দ} \bn{ড}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which two switches make the square? (\textbf{Where the tongue is}, and \textbf{whether the voice is on}.) Which letter is \textbf{\bn{ট}} with the voice switched on? (\textbf{\bn{ড}}.) And which is it with the tongue brought forward onto the teeth? (\textbf{\bn{ত}}.)

Source: \href{https://www.unicode.org/charts/PDF/U0980.pdf}{Unicode Bengali chart}.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[-ṭā]{\bn{টা} (-ṭā) — the ending that means \textquotedblleft{}the\textquotedblright{}}

\label{lesson:BN-C20-tta-classifier}



\begin{quote}
Write the letter from the lesson before, then write it with the mātrā. Then say \textbf{\bn{জামা}}.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \bn{টা}}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\bn{জামা}} — \emph{jāmā} — \textbf{shirt.}
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{\bn{জামাটা}} — \emph{jāmāṭā} — \textbf{the shirt.}
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{\bn{চা}} — \emph{chā} — \textbf{tea.}
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{\bn{চাটা}} — \emph{chāṭā} — \textbf{the tea.}
\end{quote}

Bengali has no word for \textbf{the}. Thirty chapters of this book have taught nouns that float free — \emph{shirt}, \emph{tea}, \emph{brother} — with no way to say you mean \textbf{that one, the one we are both thinking of}. The way you say it is not a word in front. It is \textbf{\bn{টা}}, stuck on the end.

Nothing goes between the noun and it, and nothing comes before the noun. The noun and its ending are written as one word.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: why this is called a classifier and not an article}]
An article does one job: it says \emph{definite}. \textbf{\bn{টা}} does that and one more. Bengali will not put a number directly on a noun, so \textbf{\bn{টা}} is also the piece a count has to pass through — you will meet that in the next lesson.

There is a polite twin, \textbf{\bn{টি}}, used for people and in careful writing:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{\bn{ভাইটা}} — \emph{bhāiṭā} — the brother, plainly
  \item \textbf{\bn{ভাইটি}} — \emph{bhāiṭi} — the brother, respectfully
\end{itemize}

Same slot, same job, different warmth. Learn \textbf{\bn{টা}} and recognise \textbf{\bn{টি}}.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{jāmāṭā} — the shirt
  \item \emph{chāṭā} — the tea
  \item \emph{bhāiṭā}, then the polite \emph{bhāiṭi}
  \item the red one — \emph{lāl jāmāṭā}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Where does \textbf{\bn{টা}} go — in front of the noun or on the end of it? (\textbf{On the end}, written as one word.) Does Bengali have a word for \textbf{the}? (\textbf{No} — this ending is what it has instead.) And which form would you use of a person you were being careful about? (\textbf{\bn{টি}}.)

Source: \href{https://www.unicode.org/charts/PDF/U0980.pdf}{Unicode Bengali chart}.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[ekṭā]{\bn{একটা} (ekṭā) — a, one}

\label{lesson:BN-C20-ekta}



\begin{quote}
Say \textbf{the shirt}. Then read \textbf{\bn{এক}}.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \bn{একটা}}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\bn{একটা} \bn{জামা}} — \emph{ekṭā jāmā} — \textbf{a shirt.}
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{\bn{একটা} \bn{বন্ধু}} — \emph{ekṭā bôndhu} — \textbf{a friend.}
\end{quote}

Chapter twenty-four taught you to count \textbf{\bn{এক} \bn{দুই} \bn{তিন} \bn{চার} \bn{পাঁচ}}, and then gave you nothing to count. This is why. \textbf{\bn{এক}} cannot sit next to a noun. Bengali makes a number reach its noun through the classifier, and \textbf{\bn{এক}} plus \textbf{\bn{টা}} is \textbf{\bn{একটা}} — which then means both \emph{one} and \emph{a}, because in Bengali those are the same thought.

So the ending you learned one lesson ago turns out to have been two doors:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{\bn{জামাটা}} — \textbf{the} shirt, the one we mean
  \item \textbf{\bn{একটা} \bn{জামা}} — \textbf{a} shirt, any one
\end{itemize}

Same \textbf{\bn{টা}}. Nothing in front of it, or a number in front of it.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: where the ending goes, and it moves}]
Watch which word carries the suffix:

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{} & \textbf{Bengali} & \textbf{the ending is on} \\
\midrule
the shirt & \textbf{\bn{জামাটা}} & the noun \\
a shirt & \textbf{\bn{একটা} \bn{জামা}} & the number \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

When a number turns up, the classifier leaves the noun and attaches to the number instead. That is one rule, and it is the rule that will carry every count you ever make in this language.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{ekṭā jāmā} — a shirt
  \item \emph{ekṭā bôndhu} — a friend
  \item the pair, back to back — \emph{jāmāṭā}, then \emph{ekṭā jāmā}
  \item a tea — \emph{ekṭā chā}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Can \textbf{\bn{এক}} stand next to a noun on its own? (\textbf{No} — it goes through the classifier.) When a number appears, which word carries \textbf{\bn{টা}}? (\textbf{The number}, not the noun.) And what two English words does \textbf{\bn{একটা}} cover? (\textbf{A}, and \textbf{one}.)

Source: \href{https://www.unicode.org/charts/PDF/U0980.pdf}{Unicode Bengali chart}.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[ārekṭā]{\bn{আরেকটা} (ārekṭā) — another one}

\label{lesson:BN-C20-arekta}



\begin{quote}
Say \textbf{a shirt}. Then say the joiner from chapter twenty-eight that means \textbf{and}.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \bn{আরেকটা}}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\bn{আরেকটা} \bn{চা}} — \emph{ārekṭā chā} — \textbf{another tea.}
\end{quote}

Take the word apart and it is already three things you own:

\textbf{\bn{আর}} (and) + \textbf{\bn{এক}} (one) + \textbf{\bn{টা}} (the classifier) $\to$ \textbf{\bn{আরেকটা}}

Which is why it does not merely mean \emph{a different one}. It means \textbf{one more}, with the \emph{and} still inside it.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: the pair that hands things out one at a time}]
Bengali uses \textbf{\bn{একটা} … \bn{আরেকটা}} as a fixed pair to run down a list of things one by one, the way English uses \emph{one … another}:

\begin{quote}
\textbf{\bn{একটা} \bn{লাল}, \bn{আরেকটা} \bn{কালো}} — \emph{ekṭā lāl, ārekṭā kālo} — \textbf{one red, another black.}
\end{quote}

This is the first time in this book that two things can be picked out and set side by side as separate items. Before the classifier existed there was no way to say \textbf{one} of anything, so there was no way to say \textbf{another} either.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{ārekṭā chā} — another tea
  \item the pair — \emph{ekṭā lāl, ārekṭā kālo}
  \item two shirts, one at a time — \emph{ekṭā jāmā, ārekṭā jāmā}
  \item the three pieces inside the word — \emph{ār}, \emph{ek}, \emph{ṭā}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What three pieces is \textbf{\bn{আরেকটা}} built from? (\textbf{\bn{আর}}, \textbf{\bn{এক}} and \textbf{\bn{টা}}.) What does the first piece add to the meaning? (\textbf{And} — so it is \emph{one more}, rather than only \emph{a different one}.) And what is the word it pairs with? (\textbf{\bn{একটা}}.)

Source: \href{https://www.unicode.org/charts/PDF/U0980.pdf}{Unicode Bengali chart}.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[-ṭā · ekṭā · ārekṭā]{One, the one, and another}

\label{lesson:BN-R20-one-and-another}



\begin{quote}
One ending arrived in this chapter and did three different jobs. Name the three, and say for each one where the ending sits.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Write it:} \bn{ট}, then \bn{টা}
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{jāmāṭā}, \emph{ekṭā jāmā}, \emph{ārekṭā jāmā}
  \item \emph{Recall:} two chapters back, the joiner that opens a clause about a moment — \emph{jôkhon}
\end{itemize}

\subsection*{Your turn: the distant band — every noun in the book, picked out one at a time}
This is what the chapter bought. Chapters ten to fifteen taught a pantry, a family, a face and a wardrobe, and not one of those nouns could be pointed at as \textbf{the} one or counted as \textbf{a} one. Every one of them can now. Take them cold, from memory.

Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item the four things you drink and eat, each as \textbf{the} one — \emph{chāṭā}, \emph{jôlṭā}, \emph{dudhṭā}, \emph{bhātṭā}
  \item the same four as \textbf{a} one — \emph{ekṭā chā}, \emph{ekṭā jôl}, \emph{ekṭā dudh}, \emph{ekṭā bhāt}
  \item the family, respectfully — \emph{bhāiṭi}, \emph{bônṭi}, \emph{bôndhuṭi}
  \item the wardrobe and its colours — \emph{lāl jāmāṭā}, \emph{kālo kāpôṛṭā}, \emph{nīl jāmāṭā}, \emph{shādā jāmāṭā}
  \item the face, one part at a time — \emph{ekṭā chokh, ārekṭā chokh}, then \emph{nākṭā}, \emph{mukhṭā}
  \item the whole family in one word — \emph{pôribārṭā}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Does Bengali have a word for \textbf{the}? (\textbf{No} — it has this ending.) When a number stands in front, which word carries the ending? (\textbf{The number}.) Which form is the careful one, for people? (\textbf{\bn{টি}}.) And which letter had to be taught before any of this chapter could be written down? (\textbf{\bn{ট}}.)

Source: \href{https://www.unicode.org/charts/PDF/U0980.pdf}{Unicode Bengali chart}.
\end{tcolorbox}
